intro: Porto's grandest trees mostly arrived with 19th-century British port wine families, who filled their quintas with tulip trees, magnolias and southern hemisphere exotics their money could import but Porto's own climate had to accept. Two gardens hold much of what is worth seeing, the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal and the Jardim Botânico do Porto. A short walk east adds three University of Porto quintas, the same collector's habit continued on academic ground. Porto also calls itself the City of Camellias, and means it literally.
meta_description: Porto's remarkable trees range from a 250-year tulip tree to three of Portugal's oldest Bischofia trees, across two gardens and three university quintas.
question_answer: Porto's oldest documented tree is a Virginia tulip tree (Liriodendron tulipifera) beside Casa Tait in the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, more than 250 years old and one of the first individual trees Portugal placed under legal protection, in 1950. It stands inside the free public gardens off Rua de D. Manuel II, a short walk from the Palácio de Cristal pavilion.
question_meta: Porto's oldest tree is a 250-year tulip tree at Casa Tait, protected since 1950. Where it stands, and the city's most remarkable trees.
question_context: The tulip tree beside Casa Tait has the strongest documented age claim in Porto: it was already mature enough to warrant individual legal protection when Portugal formalised its tree of public interest classification in 1950, and both the city council's own parks department and independent garden historians place its age at over 250 years. That makes it older than the Palácio de Cristal gardens built around it, which German landscape architect Émile David laid out in the 1860s, and older than the original glass-and-iron exhibition palace itself, demolished in 1951 and replaced with the domed arena that stands there now. Casa Tait, the mansion beside the tree, took its name from a family of British port wine merchants whose 19th-century wealth shaped much of what grows in this corner of the garden, tulip trees, magnolias and camellias among them. A second, taller tulip tree grows nearby without the same formal protection status, and should not be confused with the older, classified specimen the question above refers to.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Porto?
faq.a: A Virginia tulip tree beside Casa Tait in the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, over 250 years old and individually protected since 1950, one of Portugal's earliest such classifications.

faq.q: Are Porto's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Nearly all of them. Sixteen of the seventeen stand in free public gardens or walkable university campuses: the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, the Jardim Botânico do Porto, and three University of Porto quintas a short walk further east. The one exception is the Camphor Tree of Via Panorâmica, which stands on a privately owned plot and is viewed from the public road rather than entered.

faq.q: Why is Porto called the City of Camellias?
faq.a: Camellias, introduced from China and Japan in the 18th and 19th centuries, thrived so well in Porto's mild, humid climate that Portuguese growers began exporting specimens back to camellia breeders elsewhere in Europe. Casa Tait's own century-old camellia hedges, inside the Palácio de Cristal gardens, are among the oldest surviving examples in the city.

faq.q: Why do so many of Porto's remarkable trees grow in the same handful of gardens?
faq.a: The Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, the Jardim Botânico do Porto, and the University of Porto quintas further east (Casa Primo Madeira, the FAUP campus, Palacete Burmester) all began as private 19th-century estates belonging to wealthy families, several with ties to the port wine trade, who competed to plant the most impressive imported specimens. Nearly all later passed into public or university ownership, keeping their tree collections intact and mostly freely accessible.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Casa Tait

location.address: Casa Tait, Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Rua de D. Manuel II, 4050 Porto

trees.story: This American tulip tree became one of Portugal's first individually protected trees in 1950, a legal status most of the country's current laws postdate. It grows beside Casa Tait, a 19th-century mansion inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal that once belonged to a British port wine family, and at more than 250 years old it predates both the mansion and the palace gardens built around it by a century or more. Liriodendron tulipifera is native to the eastern United States, named for the yellow-green, cup-shaped flowers it produces each late spring, blooms that only appear once a tree reaches real maturity and can go unnoticed entirely on a younger specimen. A second tulip tree grows nearby in the same grounds, over 40 metres tall, though it lacks this one's formal protection status and shouldn't be confused with it. Porto's oldest tulip tree survived the transformation of its surrounding grounds more than once: the Palácio de Cristal itself, the glass-and-iron exhibition hall that gave the gardens their name, was demolished in 1951 and replaced by the domed sports arena still standing today, a change that came one year after this tree's own protection was made permanent. Whatever else has come and gone around it, the tulip tree has stayed exactly where it was planted.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops
trees.notes: Protection since 1950 and 250+ year age confirmed by both the Porto city council's own parks page and an independent garden-history source. Location upgraded to confirmed: the municipality's own open-data register of classified trees carries a Liriodendron tulipifera record with the exact same legal reference and 1950-09-01 classification date cited above, giving a surveyed point about 170m from the previous whole-garden estimate. A second Liriodendron tulipifera also appears in the open-data set nearby, classified separately in 2021 (a different legal reference and date), matching the story's own note about a second, less formally distinguished tulip tree in the same grounds; the 1950 record was used since it matches this tree's own citation. trees.name: The Magnolia of Casa Tait

location.address: Casa Tait, Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Rua de D. Manuel II, 4050 Porto

trees.story: The base of this southern magnolia measures more than six metres around, thick enough that it would take several adults linking arms to circle it. It grows in the same grounds as Casa Tait's protected tulip tree, inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, and like its neighbour it was formally classified a tree of public interest on 21 May 2021, a status that turns deliberate damage to it into a legal offence rather than simply bad manners. Magnolia grandiflora is native to the southeastern United States, prized in European gardens since the 18th century for its glossy, leathery leaves and dinner-plate-sized white flowers, which release a lemon-and-vanilla scent strong enough to notice from several metres away. Late summer is when this specimen puts on its best show, its last flush of blooms opening just as most of the garden's spring flowering has finished elsewhere. Casa Tait's grounds, now folded into the wider Palácio de Cristal park, once belonged to the Tait family, British port wine merchants whose 19th-century money planted much of what still grows here. The magnolia, like the tulip tree beside it, has outlasted the family's ownership by generations.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

best_time.label: August, for the season's last flush of lemon-scented white blooms

trees.name: The Metrosidero of the Library

location.address: Near Biblioteca Almeida Garrett, Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Rua de D. Manuel II, 4050 Porto

trees.story: New Zealand's Christmas tree has adapted well to a country that celebrates the holiday in December for entirely unrelated reasons. This metrosideros, a species Māori communities call pōhutukawa and prize for the blaze of red flowers it produces each southern summer, stands near the Biblioteca Almeida Garrett inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, and was formally classified a tree of public interest on 15 March 2019. In its native New Zealand the species flowers in December, coinciding with the Southern Hemisphere summer, which is how it earned its English common name; transplanted to Porto's Northern Hemisphere climate, its flowering calendar shifts to match local seasons instead. It shares this corner of the garden with a Washingtonia palm and a scattering of camellias, part of the eclectic plant collection assembled here since the gardens were laid out in the 1860s by German landscape architect Émile David. The library beside it, built decades after the original planting, inherited the metrosideros as an established feature of the grounds rather than the other way around. Most visitors walking to the library's entrance pass directly under its canopy without knowing they're standing beneath one of the southern hemisphere's most photographed flowering trees.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops
trees.notes: Location confirmed and classification status corrected: the municipality's own open-data register of classified trees shows this Metrosideros excelsa (the only one in the whole dataset, a genuinely distinctive match) was formally classified 2019-03-15, not still under review as the 2017 source that originally flagged this tree had it. trees.name: The Plane of Quinta da Macieirinha

location.address: Quinta da Macieirinha, Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Rua de Entre Quintas, 4050 Porto

trees.story: A house dedicated to a dead king's exile keeps its own protected tree in the garden outside. The London plane at Quinta da Macieirinha, a manor house inside the Palácio de Cristal park grounds now serving as Porto's Museu Romântico, is under formal review for protection as a tree of public interest alongside the palace's more famous specimens across the park. The museum inside commemorates Charles Albert of Sardinia, the abdicated King of Sardinia-Piedmont who spent the final months of his life at this house in 1849, having lost his throne after a failed war against Austria. The plane tree predates that story by decades, part of the working quinta's original planting before its owners ever imagined a deposed Italian monarch would die inside. London planes were a standard choice for 19th-century Portuguese gardens, valued for fast growth, tolerance of hard pruning, and mottled, flaking bark that sheds pollution along with old skin, part of why the species still lines so many European boulevards today. This one has grown alongside the house through its transformation from private residence to royal deathbed to public museum, three very different identities for the same modest patch of ground.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (Museu Romântico interior charges separate admission)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

trees.name: The Camellias of Casa Tait
trees.label: Ensemble

location.address: Casa Tait, Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Rua de D. Manuel II, 4050 Porto

trees.story: Porto calls itself the City of Camellias, and the oldest proof of that claim is a set of hedges, not a single tree. More than sixty camellia specimens grow around Casa Tait inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, several over a century old, planted as living, blooming partitions that section off parts of the garden the way a wall or fence would elsewhere. Camellias arrived in Portugal from China and Japan in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the country's mild, humid north proved so well suited to the plant that Portuguese growers eventually exported specimens back to camellia breeders across the rest of Europe, an unusual reversal of the typical colonial plant trade. Porto in particular leaned into the association hard enough that camellia season, roughly November through March depending on variety, now anchors a genuine tourism calendar, with garden openings and flower shows timed around peak bloom. Casa Tait's own hedges do the quieter version of that job every year: structuring the garden's paths, screening one glorieta from the next, doing exactly what a well-placed camellia has done in Portuguese gardens for two centuries. Nobody photographs a hedge the way they photograph a single dramatic tree, which may be exactly why this one has survived so many changes of garden fashion intact.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

best_time.label: January into February, near peak camellia bloom

trees.notes: Ensemble entry: over 60 camellia specimens at Casa Tait, several centenarian, confirmed by a dedicated garden-history source; Porto's 'City of Camellias' civic branding confirmed independently via the city's own environment department. No single representative specimen is named in either source, hence a group entry rather than one tree. Pin moved 2026-07-27 about 140m to Casa Tait's own building coordinates (Nominatim), the same correction applied to this garden's other Casa Tait entry; stays approximate since this is a scattered ensemble, not one trunk. Photo note (2026-07-29 spot-check): the approved image is a genuine, correctly licensed Camellia japonica bloom, but it is a generic species close-up with no tie to Casa Tait or Porto, not a photo of this specific hedge collection. Left in place since it honestly illustrates the species this entry is about and no better alternative was found on Commons (checked the Palácio de Cristal category directly, nothing camellia-specific), but flagged here so it is never mistaken for a photo of the actual garden.

trees.name: The Bischofia Trio of the Botanical Garden
trees.label: Ensemble

location.address: Jardim Botânico do Porto, Rua do Campo Alegre 1191, 4150 Porto

trees.story: Three of the oldest members of a common tropical street tree species anywhere in Portugal grow together in one Porto garden. These Bischofia javanica, a fast-growing evergreen more often planted along Asian avenues than kept in botanical collections, are estimated at 120 to 150 years old, among the oldest specimens of the species documented in the country, and Porto's city council has classified all three jointly as trees of public interest. They stand in the Jardim Botânico do Porto, the former grounds of the Campo Alegre estate before the University of Porto absorbed the property and turned its greenhouses and formal beds into a research and teaching collection now run by the university's Natural History and Science Museum. Bischofia javanica, native to South and Southeast Asia, produces small dark fruit that stains heavily when crushed, a trait that makes it common as a shade tree along tropical roads and rare as a deliberate botanical specimen in European gardens, part of why this trio's protected status matters: there are very few comparably documented examples anywhere in the country to measure them against. The garden around them holds more than 1,100 plant species across roughly four hectares, but these three, ordinary elsewhere and unusual here, are the ones with their own legal protection order.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.notes: Age range, joint classification and 'oldest of species in Portugal' status confirmed by the city council's own classification announcement; garden history and species count confirmed independently via Wikipedia. Location upgraded to confirmed: an iNaturalist observation of this species inside the garden, the only Bischofia javanica recorded there, gives a surveyed point for one of the three (Bischofia javanica being rare enough in Portugal that a species match this specific is strong corroboration), about 130m from the previous whole-garden estimate. Photo from the same observation, viewed directly: fruit clusters and foliage consistent with the species.

trees.name: The Texas Madrone of the Botanical Garden

location.address: Jardim Botânico do Porto, Rua do Campo Alegre 1191, 4150 Porto

trees.story: A tree named for Texas and Mexico has found an unlikely second home in a university garden in northern Portugal. This Arbutus xalapensis, commonly called the Texas madrone across its native range in the Trans-Pecos region and northeastern Mexico, is currently under formal review for protection as a tree of public interest at the Jardim Botânico do Porto. The species is a close relative of the strawberry tree that grows wild across Portugal's own hillsides, sharing the same reddish, peeling bark and small urn-shaped flowers, which may be exactly why it settled into this collection more easily than most of the garden's other exotic imports. Specimens of this size are rare outside their native range, since the species is notoriously difficult to cultivate away from the dry, well-drained limestone soils it evolved for, and few botanical gardens outside Texas and northern Mexico maintain a documented example at all. The Jardim Botânico do Porto occupies the former Campo Alegre estate, absorbed by the University of Porto in the 20th century and now run as a teaching and research collection alongside its role as a free public garden. This madrone is one of the collection's quieter successes: no dramatic size record, no royal history, just a temperamental species that, against the odds, has been thriving in the wrong hemisphere for years.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.notes: Classification status confirmed by the city council's announcement; general garden context via Wikipedia. No age, planting date or measurement found in either source, so age is left as unknown rather than guessed. Location upgraded to confirmed, 2026-07-29: ICNF's own national register of classified trees of public interest (BDG/AIP layer, sigservices.icnf.pt) carries an Arbutus xalapensis record (id 539) explicitly at 'Jardim Botânico da universidade do Porto', the only one in the whole city dataset, a genuinely distinctive species match; no legal classification reference is filled in yet there, consistent with this story's 'under formal review' status. Gives a surveyed point about 57m from the previous whole-garden estimate. trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Palácio de Cristal

location.address: Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Rua de D. Manuel II, 4050 Porto

trees.story: At around 24 metres tall, this Himalayan cedar is one of the largest of its species growing anywhere in Porto, a claim made cautiously since more than one Porto garden has a candidate for the title and no citywide survey has settled the question. It grows in the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, high enough on the hillside that its crown clears the rooftops below and looks out over the Douro valley, and its size alone marks it out in a garden better known for camellias and formal beds than for conifers this large. Cedrus deodara is native to the western Himalayas, where it is the national tree of Pakistan and grows at altitudes most other cedars can't tolerate, and it reached European gardens in the 19th century as one of several Himalayan conifers collectors raced to introduce once British expansion into the region made seed collection possible. Its drooping, slightly weeping branch tips distinguish it at a glance from the stiffer, more horizontal cedars of Lebanon and Atlas that grow in other Porto gardens. No precise planting date has surfaced for this specimen, only its approximate current height, so its age here is an estimate rather than a documented fact. What isn't in question is the view: few other trees in the garden let you see this much of the city at once.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops
trees.notes: Height (~24 m) and 'possibly largest in the city' claim come from one detailed garden-history source describing a Porto cedar of this size and species; softened to 'one of the largest' per hard rule 8, since a comparable claim exists for other Porto cedars and no single citywide record-holder has been confirmed. The photo's own Commons categorisation and species identification (Cedrus deodara, Jardins do Palácio de Cristal) place it specifically in this garden, which fixed the location for this entry. No age or planting date found. Checked 2026-07-29 against ICNF's national register of classified trees (sigservices.icnf.pt, BDG/AIP layer) for a surveyed point: the only Cedrus deodara record for Porto is at 'FCUP - Faculdade de Ciências da Universidade do Porto' (id 536), a campus site near the Botanical Garden, not the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal where this tree and its photo are placed, so it was not used. No better source for this pin found; stays approximate.

trees.name: The Coast Redwood of the Botanical Garden

location.address: Jardim Botânico do Porto, Rua do Campo Alegre 1191, 4150 Porto

trees.story: The tallest tree species on Earth has a foothold in a four-hectare university garden in Porto, and it's already one of the biggest specimens the city has. This coast redwood, native to a narrow fog belt along the California and southern Oregon coastline where mature wild trees exceed 100 metres, is nowhere near that scale here, but the Jardim Botânico do Porto's own description lists it among the largest sequoias documented in the city. Coast redwoods reached European botanical collections in the mid-19th century, decades after their first scientific description, and gardens across Britain, France and the Iberian Peninsula planted them as living proof of the New World's most extreme trees, with no clear sense yet of how they'd perform in a climate so different from California's summer fog. This one has thrived well enough that its crown is now a genuine landmark within the garden's skyline, visible above the surrounding conifer collection from most approaches. The species can reproduce from stump sprouts as well as seed, meaning a felled coast redwood can regrow from its own base, a trait almost no other conifer shares. Porto's specimen has needed no such resilience yet. It has simply grown, steadily, since whichever year in the garden's history someone planted a California seedling in Portuguese soil and hoped for the best.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.notes: 'Among the largest in the city' status confirmed by two independent sources describing the garden's conifer collection. No age, planting date or precise height measurement found for this individual tree, so age is left as unknown rather than guessed, still flagged for that gap. Location upgraded to confirmed: an iNaturalist observation of this species inside the garden, the only Sequoia sempervirens recorded there, gives a surveyed point about 60m from the previous whole-garden estimate. Photo from the same observation, viewed directly: a tall reddish fibrous-barked trunk rising into a conifer canopy, consistent with the species.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of the Botanical Garden

location.address: Jardim Botânico do Porto, Rua do Campo Alegre 1191, 4150 Porto

trees.story: Of the three cedar species growing in this collection, the Atlas cedar is the one a local garden writer singled out as the most beautiful, an unusually direct piece of praise to volunteer about one specimen rather than a whole species. This particular Cedrus atlantica grows in the Jardim Botânico do Porto's conifer collection, native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, a range it shares with no natural competition from either of its more famous cedar relatives, the cedar of Lebanon and the Himalayan cedar, both planted nearby in the same garden. All three species look similar enough at a distance, distinguished mainly by branch angle and needle colour, that telling them apart requires standing close enough to compare bark and cone shape directly, a small identification puzzle the garden's layout seems to invite by planting the three so near each other. Atlas cedars were introduced to European gardens in the 1840s, later than Lebanon cedars but earlier than the Himalayan species, part of a decades-long sequence of cedar introductions that let 19th-century botanists compare three ecologically similar trees from three unconnected mountain ranges within a single afternoon's walk. No individual age or measurement has surfaced for this tree beyond its standing as a mature, well-formed specimen. Its reputation here rests entirely on how it looks, which, by every account gathered, is exactly the point.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.notes: Single-source tree: the 'most beautiful in the garden' description and general presence come from one dedicated garden-history blog, and no second independent source confirming this specific specimen was found despite a real search. Kept because the underlying facts (species, general garden context, presence of a comparative cedar collection) are independently verifiable even though this exact tree isn't cross-confirmed; age left unknown rather than guessed. Checked 2026-07-29 against ICNF's national register of classified trees (sigservices.icnf.pt, BDG/AIP layer): the only Cedrus atlantica record for the whole of Porto is at 'Jardim da Casa do Professor' (id 360), a distinct site roughly 300m from the Botanical Garden's own coordinates with no clear connection to the garden in any source found, so it was not used to upgrade this pin; still approximate. Photo search 2026-07-29: no openly-licensed photo found on Wikimedia Commons (no 'Cedrus atlantica in Portugal' category exists), iNaturalist, Openverse or Flickr CC search. Still missing.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of FAUP

location.address: Faculdade de Arquitectura da Universidade do Porto (FAUP), Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso, Quinta do Gólgota, Porto

trees.story: Architects travel to this campus for the buildings. The tree was here first. This copper beech grows in the gardens of the Quinta do Gólgota, the old estate that became the Faculty of Architecture of the University of Porto, a short walk from the Casa Cor-de-Rosa and the Pavilhão Carlos Ramos. Álvaro Siza began remodelling the site in 1984, and what he built here is one of the addresses the Escola do Porto is known by, visited by architecture students from all over. The beech was already more than sixty years old when the first drawings were made. It measures 4.85 metres around at chest height, stands 23 metres tall and carries a crown 20 metres across, all measured in 2020, the year Portugal's forest institute classified it a tree of public interest on the city council's proposal and with the University's agreement as owner. Copper beech is the purple-leaved form of the common European beech, planted through the 19th century by estate owners who wanted something on the lawn that was not green. This one has outlived the fashion, the estate and the family that paid for both, and it now spends its days being photographed by accident, in the background of somebody's shot of a Siza wall. Campus hours, no ticket.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before darkening

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of Via Panorâmica

location.address: Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso (roadside, former Quinta do Gólgota), Porto

trees.story: The road came second. This camphor is very probably one of the original plantings of the Quinta do Gólgota, the 19th-century estate that Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso was later cut through, which makes it the survivor of a garden that has otherwise gone. Porto's city council says as much on its own record for the tree. Camphor is an East Asian evergreen, grown for the aromatic crystals distilled from its wood, and it reached Porto with the estate owners who collected the world's trees the way other people collected porcelain. This one measures around four metres in circumference at chest height and six at the base, stands 21 metres tall and spreads a crown roughly 20 metres wide. There is a healed wound low on the trunk, the kind a tree closes over decades, and the council records it as stable. Everything else around it has changed: the estate broken up, a scenic road driven along the Douro bluff, the Faculty of Architecture built next door, and the plot the tree stands on now in private hands with development potential on the municipal record. That last fact decides the visit. The land is not open and there is no way up to the trunk. You look at this tree from the pavement of the public road, and that is the whole of it. At that size it is enough, because from the roadside a camphor of four metres reads as a green wall.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Quinta Primo Madeira

location.address: Rua do Campo Alegre, nº 877, Quinta/Casa Primo Madeira (Pólo 3 da Universidade do Porto), Porto

trees.story: Three named architects have worked on this small garden, and the trees outlasted every plan. Casa Primo Madeira is a late 19th-century palacete on Rua do Campo Alegre, built for the textile industrialist Primo Monteiro Madeira, altered for him by José Marques da Silva, then bought by the University of Porto and restored between 1986 and 1988 by Fernando Távora, with the garden itself remodelled by the landscape architect Francisco Caldeira Cabral. Through all of it the Atlas cedar stayed exactly where it was. On 30 November 2004 Portugal's official gazette classified it a tree of public interest together with two neighbours on the same lawn, a tulip tree and a plane, which is a high concentration of protected trees for a garden this size. The cedar measures 4.05 metres around at chest height and stands about 20 metres tall, with a crown roughly as wide as it is high. Cedrus atlantica comes from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, where it is now classed as endangered in the wild while growing untroubled in park after European park, an inversion that says more about grazing and logging at home than about the tree. The house is Pólo 3 of the University today. Walk in during university hours, stand on the lawn, and all three protected trees are in sight at once.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Quinta Primo Madeira

location.address: Rua do Campo Alegre, nº 877, Quinta/Casa Primo Madeira (Pólo 3 da Universidade do Porto), Porto

trees.story: The crown of this tulip tree is wider than the tree is tall: 23.5 metres across against 21 metres of height. That shape only happens when a tree spends a century with nothing crowding it, which is precisely what the garden of Casa Primo Madeira has given it. Its trunk measures 4.35 metres around, and it was classified a tree of public interest on 30 November 2004, in the same gazette notice as the Atlas cedar and the plane standing a few paces away. Porto has more than one enormous Liriodendron tulipifera, which regularly confuses people. The famous one grows at Casa Tait in the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, protected since 1950 and considerably older. This is a different tree in a different garden about 750 metres away, planted during the same 19th-century wave of estate collecting that filled this hillside with species from other continents. Tulip trees are the tallest hardwoods of the eastern American forests and among the earliest of them to reach European gardens. The flowers, greenish with an orange band and genuinely tulip-shaped, open in June high in the crown where most visitors never spot them. The moment that carries across the whole garden comes later in the year, when a canopy that wide turns clear yellow all at once and then lets it go.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the whole crown turns clear yellow at once

trees.name: The London Plane of Quinta Primo Madeira

location.address: Rua do Campo Alegre, nº 877, Quinta/Casa Primo Madeira (Pólo 3 da Universidade do Porto), Porto

trees.story: At 6.4 metres around, this plane carries one of the thickest trunks measured anywhere in Porto. It is also the shortest of the three protected trees in the garden of Casa Primo Madeira, 17 metres tall against a crown 25 metres wide, which is the profile of a tree that never had to compete for light and put its growth sideways instead. Planes are the standard street tree of half of Europe and get treated accordingly: pollarded back to knuckles every few winters, cut clear of tram wires, kept to whatever size a pavement can hold. This one was left alone behind a wall for a century, and that difference is the reason to go and look at it. Portugal's official gazette classified it a tree of public interest on 30 November 2004, in one notice with the Atlas cedar and the tulip tree on the same lawn. The house behind it was built for the textile industrialist Primo Monteiro Madeira, acquired by the University of Porto, restored by Fernando Távora in the late 1980s, and now serves as Pólo 3, an academic building on a walkable campus that opened its doors to the public for Open House Porto in 2019. Come during university hours. The three trees stand within a minute of one another.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Palacete Burmester

location.address: Jardim do Palacete Burmester ('Casa dos Livros'), grounds of the Faculdade de Ciências, Universidade do Porto, Rua do Campo Alegre 1055, Porto

trees.story: Every conker in Europe descends from a handful of mountain ravines in Greece and Albania, the only places the horse chestnut still grows wild, and where the species is now classed as vulnerable. Everywhere else it is a planted tree, and this is one of Porto's. It stands in the garden of the Palacete Burmester, the house the University of Porto runs as the Casa dos Livros on the Faculty of Sciences campus, and in 2020 it was classified a tree of public interest along with three neighbours on the same lawn: a Himalayan cedar, a tulip tree and a yew. Four protected trees in one small garden is somebody's collection rather than an accident. How old this one is, nobody has written down. Neither Portugal's forest register nor the city council gives it a date. The register holds a single measurement, a trunk 3.15 metres around in 2020, which on this species means well over a century and stops being useful after that. So the honest version is a tree that is protected, mature and undated, and anyone quoting a year for it is guessing. The garden sits a few hundred metres from the Jardim Botânico do Porto, close enough that its redwood, its bischofias and its cedars belong on the same afternoon.

best_time.label: September and October, when the conkers ripen and drop onto the lawn

trees.name: The Yew of Palacete Burmester
trees.age_estimate: unknown, mature (large girth for the species)

location.address: Jardim do Palacete Burmester ('Casa dos Livros'), grounds of the Faculdade de Ciências, Universidade do Porto, Rua do Campo Alegre 1055, Porto

trees.story: A yew with a trunk 5.8 metres around normally comes with a documented history. This one has none. Portugal's forest register took the measurement in 2020, classified the tree, and left the age column empty; the city council's announcement lists the yew among four protected specimens in the garden of the Palacete Burmester and gives no date either. That gap is better left open than filled in. Taxus baccata thickens slowly enough that trees of this girth elsewhere in Europe are routinely dated in the several hundreds of years, so it is reasonable to think this one is old. It is not honest to print a number. Yews also make their own dating difficult by hollowing at the centre as they age, taking with them exactly the rings anyone would want to count. What can be said plainly is this: the tree stands in a small garden on the Faculty of Sciences campus of the University of Porto, beside the Casa dos Livros and a few hundred metres from the Jardim Botânico do Porto, and the species is scarce in Portugal outside the northern mountains, which makes a specimen this size in a city garden unusual. Every part of it is poisonous except the red flesh around the seed. It is evergreen, so February looks much like August, which at least settles the question of when to come.
